newsitem.title: USA: Lawyer says Reynolds made it cool to smoke.
newsitem.headline: Lawyer says Reynolds made it cool to smoke.

text.p: The plaintiff's lawyer in a wrongful death suit against R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. said Friday the late smoker Jean Connor was not a saint but that the tobacco company could not evade responsibility for her death from lung cancer.
"Who made it cool to smoke poison?" Norwood "Woody" Wilner asked the six-member jury in a 58-minute closing statement. His colleague, Ron Motley, also will address the jury.

In a courthouse crowded with tobacco liability attorneys, stock analysts and reporters, Wilner told the one-man, five-woman panel that Connor accepted her responsibility for the lung cancer that killed her in October 1995, at age 49. But he said Reynolds had never owned up to its responsibility.
"Reynolds should not be able to say 'it's all your fault, it's all your fault. We don't have any responsibility,'" he said.

Wilner described the verdict form the six-member jury will be asked to fill out, reading the key questions: "Was there negligence on the part of defendant R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. which was a legal cause of the death of decedent Jean Connor?" and "Were the cigarettes manufactured by defendant R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. unreasonably dangerous and defective and a legal cause of the death of decedent Jean Connor?"

Wilner, who last August won a $750,000 judgment against Brown and Williamson Tobacco Corp. for a smoker in a product liability case -- only the second monetary award against the tobacco industry -- told jurors that Connor was not a defendant in the case.
"She is not considered to be negligent if she is buying and using a legal product," he said.

Connor's sister, Dana Raulerson, sued Reynolds on behalf of Connor's estate and her three children. Connor began smoking as a teenager and developed a three-pack-a-day habit during 35 years of smoking.

Wilner told jurors that they would be asked to punish Reynolds for selling a dangerous and defective product by awarding punitive damages. It is the first time a Florida jury is being asked to award such damages.
"We're asking you to send a message in this case. We're asking you to send a message to R.J. Reynolds and many people will hear that message."

He used graphs and charts to describe to jurors how lung cancer rates had risen dramatically even while rates of other types of cancer were falling, and said Reynolds had not only failed to warn customers that it was selling poison but had actually tried to hide tobacco's potential health hazards.

"They never labelled it hazardous. They never told anyone what was in it," he said. "They negligently marketed it. They put up beautiful pictures (in ads) ... when they knew those people were holding a keg of dynamite to the chromosomes of their cells."

Closing arguments were expected to last five hours. The jury could begin deliberations late Friday. R.J. Reynolds, whose brands include Camel, Winston and Salem, is a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp., the nation's second biggest cigarette maker.
